newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Scott sees problems in NZ treasury portfolio - NZPA.
newsitem.headline: Scott sees problems in NZ treasury portfolio - NZPA.

text.p: Former Treasury secretary Graham Scott said on Wednesday he was astounded the government gave the Treasury portfolio to New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, which he said raised questions for policy development.

He said New Zealand had experienced two "meltdowns" in relationships between prime ministers and finance ministers in its recent history and the lesson was that policy development only went smoothly when the two worked well together.

He believed Treasury would handle the split portfolio professionally and the department had had experience of disagreements about policy between finance ministers and associate or deputy finance ministers in the past.

"I have to say that I was astounded that a government that got 34 percent in the (election) polls has given the finance portfolio to the leader of a party with 13 percent (NZ First)," Scott told the New Zealand Press Association.
"I just couldn't conceive that they would give away the finance portfolio," Scott said.
Scott was Treasury secretary from 1987 to 1993 and now works as a consultant. He published a book on government reform in New Zealand on behalf of the International Monetary Fund in October.
"Obviously the two men have had a terrible relationship over the years.

"In my experience working for both the Labour government and also for the National government for the first three years and watching the performance of the government with Bill Birch as minister of finance I reached a conclusion a long time ago that economic policy development goes smoothly when a prime minister and a minister of finance are really working well together.
"And it's a disaster for a government when the prime minister and the minister of finance fall out.

"We really need to see the fine print of what they are agreeing to about economic policy because if they have left major issues about which they disagree to be resolved then we run a serious risk about the sort of meltdown we have seen in recent years when a prime minister and a minister of finance fall out."

He said that after 1987 then finance minister Roger Douglas and associate minister of finance Michael Cullen fell out and former finance minister Ruth Richardson had also disagreed with her associate minister Wyatt Creech.
"That made it very, very difficult for treasury officers who were at times forced into situations where they were advising parties to both sides of a very difficult argument.
"It's quite difficult because the civil servants are aware that this is going on and you get into difficulties about being told by one minister not to pass a paper on to another."
Prime Minister Jim Bolger said this morning on Radio Pacific that Peters would take about half the workload from the finance minister's portfolio. Bill Birch is to be finance minister.
He said the dual role of treasurer and finance minister would be a 50-50 split.
"We normally have a minister of finance and an associate minister of finance.
"Winston Peters and Bill Birch for example will work jointly on bringing together this year's budget.
"I think it is a very sensible arrangement and I think it's going to be a pretty formidable team," he said.
Scott said that the wording of the new policy targets agreement between the Reserve Bank and the government was "clever".
The agreement recognises that inflation can move outside a new target of 0-3 percent in response to price shocks.

It requires the bank to implement policy "with the intention of maintaining stability in the general level of prices, so that monetary policy can make its maximum contribution to sustainable growth, employment and development opportunities".
"What they have done is say that the bank has to pursue price stability in order to achieve those things."
"That looks like a cunning compromise," Scott said.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
